chapter: Society bands and white New Orleans attitudes
title: Race records and their Negro market
summary: Race records sold only to the Negro population and were not stocked in white music shops.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: They didn't consider that at all. It was just something for them to dance by. As for listening to records, I think it annoyed them to listen to that type of records. In fact, in New Orleans, I think you'll find, aside from the race records, it sold to the Negro population, which was comparatively late when they discovered that there was a fine market. It was 19, probably 18 or 19, before the real race records came out. And then they weren't even put in the white music shops, like Green Walls and Well Irons. Not that they were advised to them, because they had no sale among the white people.
And the race records were, of course?
They were strictly for Negroes, and they sold like hotcakes there, a very big market among the Negro population here.
It was all Negroes, both singers and players on those records.
